articles.title: First Children's Booker prize reveals shortlist ' full of surprises' - and its child judges
articles.summary: The eight books in contention include War by Artemis Fowl author Eoin Colfer  and Andrew Donkin.
articles.body:
The first ever Children's Booker Prize has announced the eight books in the running for the new £50,000 award.

Five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories are on the shortlist, which is aimed at children aged eight to 12.

The authors in contention include former Children's Laureate of Ireland Eoin Colfer, who is best known for his Artemis Fowl series, and teacher and children's author Catherine Bruton.

Four children have also been announced as new judges after a UK-wide competition. Twelve-year-old Ibrahim from Hampshire was one of those picked from more than 4,000 entrants.

He told me he was called back into school for a phone call with chair of judges Frank Cottrell-Boyce, who broke the news. Ibrahim said he couldn't be happier.

"First Children's Booker Prize judge! On my CV - that's going to take me a long way… I'm too overwhelmed to even be excited."

Cottrell-Boyce told the BBC "it's really, really important that this is a prize for children's books. Having judges who are children will be proof of that… If the children don't love a book, it won't win."

Ibrahim, his fellow child judges and Cottrell-Boyce will be joined on the judging panel by Ghosts and Horrible Histories actor Lolly Adefope and Sanchita Basu De Sarkar, who owns an award-winning children's book shop in north London.

Ibrahim said he loves reading "because it's just a way to unwind yourself from the outside world. If you get stuck in a book, you're not getting your face out of there until you finish it".

He's far too professional to share which books on the list he likes best, but he told me when he was reading one of them recently: "I had to tell my mum to confiscate it because I couldn't stop reading it and I was getting a headache."

Cottrell-Boyce said he isn't concerned over whether the adult judges might dominate the decision-making.

"If - like me - you've been visiting schools as a children's writer for 20 years, it's a rare thing to meet a child who is too over-awed to express an opinion. They're usually very forthright".

Ibrahim proves that point. He told me "the adults are not going to control that meeting… 100% not!"

He's looking for "something that has different perspectives, you can see it in a different way. New characters, not just the same old sloppy characters that authors make all the time. They just make these books that just have the same plot line".

The shortlisted books are by authors and illustrators from the UK, Ireland, Australia and Italy. Cottrell-Boyce described the list as "full of surprises." Here it is:

The Worst Thing That Could Possibly Happen by Guy Bass, illustrated by David Roberts. Readers on Goodreads describe it as "super creepy" and "how horror for kids should be written."

War by Eoin Colfer and Andrew Donkin, illustrated by Giovanni Rigano. It's the third book in their graphic novel series and tells the story of 14-year old Kat, living under siege in an unnamed European city.

The Night I Borrowed Time by Iqbal Hussain - the British-Pakistani author and former journalist's debut Children's book weaves a story through the eyes of Zubair, a seventh son who has inherited the power of time travel and tries to fix the lives of his family.

The Rambler's Curse by Mikey Please - the fantasy-comedy by the Aardman animator, who has also illustrated the book, has been described by The Guardian as a "laugh-out-loud, shaggy-dog spiral of purposes mistook".

The Teller of Tall Tales by Liz Hyder, illustrated by Tom de Freston, was a critic's choice in The Daily Telegraph. It's about a grandmother living in a remote cabin who weaves mysterious stories for her estranged grandson.

Tadpole Summer by Catherine Bruton is about a young girl who seeks solace in nature when her brother's serious illness worsens.

Séamus Almost Famous by Jessica Scott-Whyte - this is the Irish author's second book and is illustrated by Becka Moor. Poor Séamus is on a mission to emerge from the shadows of his family - even his baby sister is an accidental internet sensation.

Hometown by Australian Shaun Tan tells the story of a girl living on a distant planet who is one day told by a visitor in a spacesuit that she is actually from somewhere very far away. A review in The Observer called it "perfect fuel for a voracious imagination".

Cottrell-Boyce told the BBC the range of subjects was "amazing".

"Children's books can be about anything, can deal with anything. But the tone has to convey hope. I can't think of a darker childhood than the one endured by Anne of Green Gables. I also can't think of a more joyous book than Anne of Green Gables."

He acknowledges the worrying statistics on reading. The National Literacy Trust's Annual Literacy Survey last year showed the percentage of children and young people who said they enjoyed reading was its lowest in 20 years. Just one in three aged eight to 18 said they enjoyed reading in their free time, down by more than a third since 2005.

"That's why we're here! To fight the fight. To make sure our children have as many opportunities as possible to discover how pleasurable, how bonding, how thrilling and enriching and fortifying it can be to slip out of the prison of the present into the infinity of the story."

Ibrahim told me "my friends don't read books at all".

He doesn't try to persuade them. "I let them live their life. I live my life".

But if he were to try to, what would he say?

"Put a timer on your phone, make sure it's blocked and then they'll decide to do something more productive. I might be able to convince them... because it can help you with English, your confidence, and help you build self esteem."

For him, though, the best thing about a book is when it takes him into another world. "If you try to take your head out of it, it makes you think 'oh my god what's going to happen next?'"

The winning book will be announced in February next year at the Young V&A in London. 30,000 copies of the shortlisted books will be given to children who need them most.

articles.title: Voters barely care about climate change, but Democrats push it anyway
articles.summary: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's "Green New Deal" gains ground as six Democratic Socialists head to Congress and a well-funded climate movement eyes influence.
articles.body: As power shifts in Congress, climate extremism is poised to rise like a phoenix from the ashes. Sure, it was not a top 10 issue among voters — registering at just 1% in a September Fox News survey. Nor was it a major talking point from liberal candidates trying to find "affordability" religion after their abdication during the Biden years. But climate is the ideal Trojan horse to deliver a big government agenda without the bitter taste of socialism. Here are three reasons the blue wave could fuel a green hurricane: SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES' The climate ranks are growing During the opening weeks of the last Democratic takeover of the House in 2019, then-freshman New York Democrat Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced her so-called "Green New Deal." Its goal was as simple as it was unachievable: "meeting 100 percent of the power demand in the United States through clean, renewable, and zero-emission energy sources" while eliminating fossil fuels and phasing out nuclear energy. NEWSOM ADMITS DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST IDEAS ‘MAINSTREAM’ IN DEMOCRAT PARTY: ‘PRETTY ALIGNED’ Ocasio-Cortez channeled the fears of many of her followers by intoning, "The world is going to end in 12 years if we don't address climate change." Nearly eight years later, AOC is still in Congress, and the world is still standing. Yet now she is no longer the crazy outlier. Her views have become mainstream, at least in her party. As many as six Democratic Socialists of America members of the House will join Ocasio-Cortez on Capitol Hill next year, quadrupling the size of their ranks. THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ARE NO LONGER ON THE FRINGE Like AOC, their priorities are clear. Rep.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier, Ocasio-Cortez’s fellow New Yorker, includes the Green New Deal on her "Day One Agenda." In Michigan, Rep.-elect Donovan McKinney described his district as the "poster child for communities in need of the Green New Deal." In California, Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres is calling for "a community-driven Green New Deal." So loud is the AOC buzz that some are already collecting signatures for the 2028 presidential contest, and there is no AOC without a Green New Deal. DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT Climate is catch-all for failed governance After years of Republican leadership, Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada, Alaska and Iowa will be run by Democrats. Few challenges test chief executives more than government responses to natural disasters. When questions arise about decision-making, it is far easier to blame external factors than accept responsibility. In 2025, amid the blaze that claimed more than 6,000 homes in the Palisades, California Democrat Gov. Gavin Newsom declared, "If you don’t believe in science, believe your own damn eyes." Never mind the overgrown forests and lack of brush clearance by the state agency. Or the offline water reservoir. Or the man "who is charged with starting in January 2025 what eventually became the Palisades Fire." Dare raise any of those factors and face accusations of ignoring the "science." When catastrophic flooding tragically took the lives of 136 people in Texas last year, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott downplayed the blame game. Instead of finger-pointing, he noted, "Every football team makes mistakes," and The New York Times chided him for invoking a football analogy. JOHN YOO, MICHAEL TOTH: ALOHA STATE LAWSUITS PUSH RADICAL CLIMATE AGENDA So loud is the AOC buzz that some are already collecting signatures for the 2028 presidential contest, and there is no AOC without a Green New Deal. With Democrats ascendant in Texas and elsewhere, the left will have fewer Republicans to kick around anymore. When tragedy strikes, they will need a new villain. The green in climate means cash SUPREME COURT BEGINS NEW TERM WITH HIGH-PROFILE LOOK AT CLEAN AIR AND FEDERAL AUTHORITY The left likes to howl about so-called "dark money." The first line of Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign rallying cry was a pledge to get "Money Out of Politics." Yet campaigns are not free, and the climate movement has become a thriving industry. In 2024, the League of Conservation Voters turned heads by announcing a $120 million investment in support of Democratic candidates. There are more than 34,000 climate and environmental organizations operating in the United States, employing more than 130,000 people and generating a combined nearly $30 billion in annual revenue. Lawsuits are potentially powerful and reliable revenue streams. By early 2026, more than 30 climate-damage actions brought by states, counties and cities were pending nationwide. These suits target the energy industry, drive up costs for ratepayers and help bankroll the political infrastructure that elects supportive public officials. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Newly elected Republican Wyoming Sen.-elect Harriet Hageman has pending legislation called the "Stop Climate Shakedowns Act of 2026" to prevent damaging lawsuits based on dubious science. The outgoing Congress would be wise to pass it before time expires on Republican majorities. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The underlying conditions are there for a green hurricane. A larger bloc of Democratic Socialists have prioritized the Green New Deal. Democratic governors will have incentives to blame climate rather than governance. And a well-funded climate advocacy complex will keep the pressure and lawsuits coming. Voters may have ranked climate near the bottom of their wish list in September. In Washington next year, it is unlikely to stay there. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE BY DANIEL TURNER

articles.title: Ravens cornerback T.J. Tampa has made the case for more snaps
articles.summary: Ravens defensive coordinator Jesse Minter praises young defenders T.J. Tampa and Mike Green for their recent growth.
articles.body:
The Ravens ' defense has plenty to address, but there have also been individual performances worth building on. Two young players who have caught Jesse Minter's attention are cornerback T.J. Tampa and outside linebacker Mike Green.

T.J. Tampa Jr. picked off Bryce Young in the end zone in Sunday's 35-33 loss at Carolina, but the play two snaps earlier told Jesse Minter something about how the Ravens cornerback handled a larger role. Minter singled out Tampa's coverage on a slant off a run-pass option, then pointed to his tackling and other coverage snaps. The Ravens coach said Monday that Tampa had earned the right to be on the field.

"I thought T.J. [Tampa] took advantage of the opportunity to play more. I thought, man, the play two plays before the interception, [was a] great play as well, particularly where they're at and [when they were] just trying to throw like the run-pass option slant there. [That was a] great play by him there. [There were] another couple good coverage reps as well. [He's a] physical player [and] tackles well. I thought he held up his own and did some good things. There's probably a play or two that he'd like back, but [he] certainly has earned the right to be on the field."

That is an encouraging endorsement for Tampa, who is looking to turn his opportunities into a more consistent role. Minter acknowledged that there were still things to clean up, but he clearly liked what he saw.

Green has also been making an impact, recording four sacks over the previous two games. Garrett Downing asked what has allowed the young pass rusher to find success getting after the quarterback, and Minter credited Green's physical approach and ability to work with his teammates to create pressure.

"Well, I think [Mike Green] plays really hard and physical. He gives you everything he's got from a physical standpoint. He strikes people in the run game. There are times where he's taking on a lot bigger bodies, and he's holding his own, and then he does things in the pass rush game where he works well with other guys. He works well within games. [There was] one [play] where he was setting a pick for another guy, but then he ended up kind of coming through there and getting the pressure. So, he's playing really physical. He's a good pass rusher. He's shown those skills previously and now he's taking advantage of his opportunities. He's playing a lot. I really like the way Mike's playing; I really like the way he's developed. He's certainly a bright spot."

The Ravens need more consistent production from their defense, and contributions from younger players could help them get there. Tampa and Green are showing signs of progress, giving Baltimore two players it can continue to build around.
authors: Steve Rudden and Glenn Erby , Ravens Wire

articles.title: Rory McIlroy misses out on PGA Tour Player of the Year shortlist: Who has been nominated for the Jack Nicklaus Award?
articles.summary: Wyndham Clark, Matt Fitzpatrick, Chris Gotterup, Scottie Scheffler and Cameron Young  have been shortlisted for the PGA Tour's Player of the Year award; Scheffler looks to break Tiger Woods' record by winning the Jack Nicklaus Award for a fifth consecutive season
articles.body:
McIlroy became the first player since Tiger Woods to win at Augusta National in successive years , following his one-shot victory over Scottie Scheffler, with the world No 2 adding three further top-four finishes on the PGA Tour during the season.

The six-time major champion is a three-time winner of the Jack Nicklaus Award but a noticeable absentee on the five-man shortlist for the 2026 season, announced Tuesday after being finalised by the PGA Tour Player Directors and the Player Advisory Council (PAC).

Wyndham Clark, Matt Fitzpatrick, Chris Gotterup, Scottie Scheffler and Cameron Young were the five players nominated, with the Player of the Year award then decided by votes from PGA Tour members who have played at least 15 tournaments over the season.

Scheffler won three times on the PGA Tour this season , including The American Express and two of the three FedExCup Playoffs, with the world No 1 looking to break another Woods record by winning the award for a fifth consecutive year.

The 30-year-old added five runner-up finishes over the campaign and won the Byron Nelson Award for the low scoring average, with Scheffler a strong contender despite failing to add to his major tally in 2026.

Clark won the US Open for a second time and added two further victories during the campaign, lifting him inside the world's top five, while Fitzpatrick also enjoyed three wins in his best PGA Tour season to-date.

Gotterup also picked up three wins and contended in multiple other events, with Presidents Cup team-mate Cameron Young completing the list after winning The Players and the Cadillac Championship.

Voting will close December 4, with the winners of the award and the Arnold Palmer Award for the PGA Tour Rookie of the Year then announced before the start of the 2027 season.

Viktor Hovland won the Travelers Championship and finished runner-up at the season-ending Tour Championship, while major winners Aaron Rai and Ryan Fox were among the others to miss out on the shortlist.

Fitzpatrick brothers both shortlisted for PGA Tour awards

English duo Alex Fitzpatrick and Marco Penge are among the five nominees for the Arnold Palmer Award for Rookie of the Year, having both enjoyed breakthrough wins on their maiden PGA Tour seasons.

Fitzpatrick partnered older brother Matt to victory at the Zurich Classic of New Orleans and was one of only two rookies to qualify for the Tour Championship, finishing fourth in the FedExCup rankings.

Penge retained his PGA Tour playing status in dramatic fashion at the RSM Classic, winning the final event of the FedExCup Fall in a play-off to break inside the top 100 in the season-long standings.

Norway's Kristoffer Reitan won the Truist Championship and rising star Jackson Koivun claimed the 3M Open in just his third professional start, while Ben James - a two-time runner-up in 2026 - complete the rookie quintet nominated.

articles.title: IBM to H-1B visa and green card holders in its biggest division: You can leave the company by end of 2026 as we are ending...
articles.summary: IBM is ending US visa and green card sponsorship for most roles in IBM Consulting, its biggest division with more than 150,000 employees.
articles.body: IBM is ending US visa and green card sponsorship for most roles in IBM Consulting, its biggest division with more than 150,000 employees. Workers affected by the change can either move to an IBM role outside the US or leave the company by the end of the year, Bloomberg first reported, citing a document shared with managers in the unit.The company has confirmed the decision. "IBM Consulting participates in U.S. high-skilled visa programs to address skill shortages," an IBM spokesperson said, adding that this participation had been declining for a number of years. "As skill availability and client need have evolved, we have opted to discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of such roles in IBM Consulting."IBM's H-1B workers get three weeks to choose between relocating and leavingThe choice is not an easy one. Employees get three weeks to decide, according to Sunguk Moon, CEO of anonymous workplace forum Blind. Those who don't take a role abroad get three months of severance, with December 31 as their last day. Many heard about it in what was set up as a one-on-one "career sync" with their manager.Relocating comes with its own price. One IBM employee wrote on Blind that moving to India could mean a pay cut of roughly 80%.Most of the openings are in one country too. On November 19, IBM's careers portal listed 1,278 consulting roles outside the US, of which 1,125 were in India, 23 in Singapore and 18 in the UK. The US had 89.IBM does not share how its workforce is split by country, so the exact number of people affected is unclear. Federal records show the company had just over 1,600 H-1B petitions approved in fiscal year 2026, down from over 2,000 in FY2025 and nearly 3,000 in FY2024. These numbers cover all of IBM, not only consulting, and include extensions for existing staff.Trump administration's H-1B visa crackdown is reshaping how tech companies hireThe move comes amid tight scrutiny of foreign tech hiring by the Donald Trump administration. Last month, it suspended Microsoft, Adobe and several major outsourcers, including Cognizant, Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services, from the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) process, Reuters reported. PERM is a key step for companies sponsoring foreign workers for green cards. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the suspensions, and Microsoft has publicly defended its hiring of international talent.In September 2025, the White House announced a one-time $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions, though the measure has since been tied up in the courts. The administration has also proposed changes to the annual H-1B lottery that would favour employers paying the highest salaries.Indian professionals stand to feel this the most. Indian nationals typically receive about three-quarters of all H-1B visas, and their wait for a green card can stretch to several decades, according to the National Foundation for American Policy.IBM Consulting's flat growth sits behind the sponsorship cutOver the past few years, IBM has rebuilt itself as a software company through big acquisitions such as Red Hat, HashiCorp and Confluent. Consulting, by far its largest unit, has not kept up. The division's growth has been largely flat since 2024, as per Bloomberg, and its revenue stayed at $5.3 billion in the third quarter, up 2% at constant currency.IBM's 2025 annual report put the company's total headcount at 264,300 employees across IBM and its wholly owned subsidiaries.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: WTGL: Charley Hull 'has great laugh' on Atlanta Drive debut despite defeat to Lottie Woad's Boston Common
articles.summary: Charley Hull off to Disney World after making first appearance at the SoFi Center; Englishwoman wins her opening singles match, against Solheim Cup team-mate Celine Boutier, but Atlanta Drive soundly beaten by Boston Common; watch every WTGL match live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
English star Hull won her first singles match in the competition, beating Solheim Cup team-mate Celine Boutier as she holed a 15-foot return putt having shot an initial effort way past the hole.

But Atlanta Drive were still soundly defeated in their first game of the inaugural women's season as Boston Common bounced back from last week's loss to Motor City.

Still Hull, who smoked her opening tee shot 264 yards, thoroughly enjoyed the experience, saying: "Obviously it wasn't the result that we wanted, but we had a great laugh. I know we're not on the golf course, but you're in the golf environment."

Hull's first experience of the WTGL came after a whirlwind few days in which she finished tied 23rd at the LPGA's season-ending Tour Championship and then took part in a shoot with equipment manufacturer TaylorMade.

The 30-year-old said she was "massively flagging" but will now enjoy some downtime with her family at Disney World.

Woad, whose spectacular chip-in against Motor City had taken that clash into overtime, recorded a singles victory over Atlanta's Nataliya Guseva on Tuesday evening.

With Ina Yoon also thumping Andrea Lee, Boston picked up four points to Atlanta's one in the singles having opened up a 4-2 lead after the triples leg.

Yoon secured the win for Boston when she landed her tee shot at the par-three 14th to inside three feet, earning three points with two Hammers in play.

Earlier on, Boutier chipped in from just off the green to put Boston 4-0 up after eight holes of triples before Atlanta chalked up their first two points at the ninth.

The WTGL continues with a double header on Sunday, live on Sky Sports , as Woad's Boston play New York from 6pm UK before Hull's Atlanta Drive meet unbeaten Motor City from 8.30pm UK.

articles.title: Casandra Alexander: Ladies European Tour Order of Merit winner on 'holes in the system' for players to earn LPGA cards
articles.summary: Casandra Alexander has won the Ladies European Tour Order of Merit after three wins and five runner-up finishes in 2026; Alexander secured her LPGA Tour card via Q-Series ahead of the season-ending Andalucía Costa del Sol Open de Espana, live on Sky Sports Golf
articles.body:
Alexander is inside the world's top 30, has won three times on the Ladies European Tour this season and wrapped up the Order of Merit title with two events to spare, yet still needed to negotiate Final Qualifying to secure her LPGA Tour card for next season.

The South African has been a dominant force on the LET this season, posting five runner-up finishes before following KPMG Women's Irish Open victory with further wins at the Buccellati Ladies Italian Open and Wistron Ladies Open.

PGA Tour membership is offered in the men's game via the DP World Tour's Race to Dubai rankings, with the top 10 - not already exempt - earning their card this season, whereas top LET performers still need to earn LPGA cards via their Q-Series.

"It's definitely a little disappointing," Alexander admitted to Sky Sports . "There's not one person to blame - there's structures in place and I think it just shows the holes in the structure that we need to change.

"There's a lot that goes into it, but it was also a proving point for me this year, to get my world ranking as high as possible. I was hoping to break into the top 20 and go 'really, guys, are we still going to say there's only one way to get a card and that's Q-School?'

"We need to fix the system and we need to work together, because we want the best players in the world playing against the best players in the world and all having that opportunity."

Alexander enters the season-ending Andalucía Costa del Sol Open de Espana without a practice round having safely negotiated LPGA Qualifying, finishing Monday, where a final-round 64 helped secure her card on the American circuit next season.

"I'm not saying we need to hand out [LPGA] cards, but there surely has to be more than one pathway to earn it?" Alexander added. "I don't think the point of it is to say, 'oh, look at this, it's absolute rubbish', which it is, it's going, 'cool, but how do we do better?'

"I'm sure I wouldn't have the same attitude if I didn't get my card. I went there, I got my card, but how do we do better for the next people coming through? Because this isn't going to sustain itself - you're going to lose great players over this.

"A lot say the top three or top five on the LET Order of Merit should get cards - that's not necessarily how it starts. I think the conversation starts around 'how do I play my way into LPGA events, into gaining points and into potentially getting a full card?'

"It also shows that we need to be line-up with world ranking points because I don't understand how I was 23rd in the world and could play every major but couldn't play a general LPGA Tour event - that shows another hole in the system.

"We need to have a 'top 100 in the world' spot for any LPGA event. We have that on the LET and that would have given me opportunity to play eight or nine LPGA events this year. I hope someone else doesn't get stuck in the same situation I did in the future."

Alexander was keen to taper expectations heading into the season finale, given she only arrived in Spain the day before the tournament and without her luggage, although she is keen to enjoy the experience and celebrate an impressive season.

"I felt a little lighter leaving Alabama with the [LPGA Tour] card in my hands," Alexander admitted. "We're just coming in this week to have fun. We'll give it our best and I think it's important to show face as winner of the Order of Merit at the final event - that shows a lot of character.

"I'd love to be at home celebrating but, at the same time, it's going to be a fun week. There's the award ceremony afterwards and I think now I can take it all in. We've got a lot to do and a lot to plan [for 2027], and it's very exciting.

"It has been a really big, successful year. A lot learned and I have a great team around me that I can be thankful for, for all these achievements. It's a bit surreal, but still so much I want to do."

articles.title: Grab a Meta Quest 3S With Golf+ for Under $300 at Amazon Now for Black Friday
articles.summary: It's a great option if you're looking to get into VR, or want to upgrade an old headset.
articles.body:
If you've been out of the VR scene for a minute, you might not realize just how many competitive standalone headsets there are nowadays. Between the highly sought-after Valve Steam Frame , the recently announced Meta VR Glasses , and the lineup of Meta Quest headsets , there's quite a spectrum to choose from depending on your needs.

The Meta Quest 3S, released in 2024, is still the latest headset from Meta, taking over as the new entry-level headset following the discontinuation of the Meta Quest 2. It's a great option if you're looking to get into VR, or want to upgrade an old headset. Even better, it's currently on sale for 15% off the regular price as part of Amazon's Black Friday sale . Check out the full rundown below for more details.

The Meta Quest 3S is a blend between the current flagship Meta Quest 3 and the previous generation Meta Quest 2, offering a great entry into VR for just about anyone. The Quest 3S features the same Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2 chip with 8GB RAM as the Quest 3, allowing you to play any modern VR game without issues.

As a way to reduce the overall cost a bit, the Quest 3S features a lower resolution display (the same as the Quest 2, in fact) and uses the older Fresnel lenses, which make the headset slightly bulkier than that of the Quest 3. However, it does allow for full-color passthrough, making this a great mixed reality headset.

While Meta has a number of Black Friday bundles available for the Quest 3S, the absolute lowest price option available is $297 for the 128GB model, which also includes Golf+ (a $30 value) and 1,800 in-game credits (a $10 value) which can be used to purchase additional courses. This deal is available now through November 30 and is likely the best discount we'll see for the rest of 2026.

Matthew Adler has written for IGN since 2019 covering all things gaming, tech, tabletop games, and more. You can follow him on the site formerly known as Twitter @MatthewAdler and watch him stream on Twitch .

articles.title: Australian PGA Championship: Min Woo Lee loses club after lesson with F1's Carlos Sainz and Lance Stroll
articles.summary: Min Woo Lee shoots a four-under par 68 despite being left without his eight-iron for the first round of the Australian PGA Championship after he gave a golf lesson to Formula 1 stars Carlos Sainz and Lance Stroll.
articles.body:
Australian PGA Championship - first round leaderboard

8 H Barron (Aus); -6 K Kobori (Aus), MJ Maguire (US)

Selected others: -4 MW Lee (Aus), S Scott (Sco); -3 T McKibbin (NI), C Syme (Sco); -2 W Enefer (Eng), T Lewis (Eng); -1 C Smith (Aus)

Min Woo Lee was missing his eight-iron for the first round of the Australian PGA Championship after he gave a golf lesson to Formula 1 stars Carlos Sainz and Lance Stroll - but still managed to finish four shots off the lead.

The Australian was in Las Vegas for the most recent round of the F1 calendar, with Sainz finishing the race eighth for Williams and Stroll in 17th place for Aston Martin.

"Funny story, I was with Carlos Sainz and Lance Stroll and I was giving them a lesson and I think they were touching the clubs and it's gone somewhere, so I had no eight-iron," said Lee.

"The third hole of the day I needed an eight-iron, I needed it a few times today.

"It's actually a really fun way to play golf - it's either a nine-iron I got to hit it harder or I've got to add some spin with a seven-iron."

Lee carded a four-under par 68 at the DP World Tour event in an opening round that included five birdies and a bogey as he finished four shots behind leader Haydn Barron.

"I felt like I hit really good shots, better shots than I would have with an eight-iron so I wasn't stressing.

"It's here now, we just got the update that it's here in Sydney at the house so, hopefully, I hit it better tomorrow maybe not I might keep it out."

images.caption: Image caption, Sainz (left) and Stroll (right) got together with Lee at the Las Vegas Grand Prix

articles.title: Min Woo Lee blames F1 drivers for missing eight-iron during first round of DP World Tour season opener in Australia
articles.summary: Haydn Barron holds a two-shot lead after the opening round of the BMW Australian PGA Championship; Min Woo Lee is four strokes back after blaming Carlos Sainz and Lance Stroll for missing an eight-iron; watch throughout the week live on Sky Sports Golf
articles.body:
The Australian lives in Las Vegas, where he gave a golf lesson to Williams driver Carlos Sainz and Aston Martin rival Lance Stroll last week ahead of Las Vegas GP.

Lee fired a four-under 68 during the opening round of the DP World Tour's season-opening BMW Australian PGA Championship in Sydney, despite not having an eight-iron since that session with the two F1 drivers.

"I was with Carlos Sainz and Lance Stroll and I was giving them a lesson and I think they were just touching the clubs and it's gone somewhere," Lee said.

"I needed it a few times but it's actually a really fun way to play golf: it's either a nine iron and I've got to hit it harder or add some spin with a seven iron."

Lee sits four strokes behind shock leader Haydn Barron, who posted nine birdies - including on all of the par-fives - and carded the lowest round of his DP World Tour career during an eight-under 64.

Barron holds a two-shot lead at The Lakes Golf Course over American MJ Maguire and New Zealander Kazuma Kobori, who both posted opening-round 66s, with seven players - including ex-LIV Golf player Michael La Sasso - part of the group on five under.

Cameron Smith made an underwhelming start on his first start on the DP World Tour since the collapse of LIV Golf, with the former Open champion mixing three birdies with two bogeys during his opening-round 71.

Smith is among nine players who have signed agreements with the DP World Tour to receive invites to a specific number of tournaments this season, with Carlos Ortiz - another ex-LIV golfer - also in the group on one under.

articles.title: Golf: Nick Faldo urges LIV stars to 'chip in' for unpaid firms
articles.summary: The six-time major winner calls on those who benefited financially from LIV Golf to help small businesses still owed money by the tour.
articles.body:
Sir Nick Faldo has suggested , external those who financially benefited from LIV Golf should "chip in and take care of" businesses owed money by the Saudi-backed tour.

His comments have been welcomed by UK companies still waiting to be paid.

A BBC Sport investigation found that LIV paid millions to players and executives in the weeks before filing for bankruptcy, while bills from suppliers were already overdue.

Faldo - arguably Britain's greatest golfer - said the controversial breakaway tour risked "ruining the small businesses that help make their events possible".

"British suppliers who cleaned venues and kept events running are still owed hundreds of thousands of pounds," added the six-time major winner.

"Maybe if those on and off the golf course feel they were overcompensated for their worth, they should chip in and take care of this matter."

Since the investigation was published, more firms have contacted us about money they are owed by LIV.

They include sports communications company Soapbox, which works with the likes of Anthony Joshua and Luke Littler and is owed tens of thousands of pounds.

"I'm incredibly grateful to Sir Nick Faldo for speaking out," said Krissi Foskett, whose cleaning company BD365 Clean is £75,225 out of pocket.

"For the last couple of months I've felt powerless. Having someone of his standing recognise the injustice of what's happening to businesses like ours genuinely means a lot.

"Sir Nick's suggestion that those who have benefited financially could contribute towards paying the outstanding suppliers is something I wholeheartedly welcome."

LIV Golf has not responded to requests for comment on the original investigation or Faldo's remarks.

In August, chief executive Scott O'Neil said he hoped the tour would be able to pay its suppliers.

"What I would say to them is we're doing everything we can to make sure we can do right by them and the work they committed.

"I come from a family of entrepreneurs, a family of small business entrepreneurs and know the challenge."

Faldo's one-time on-course rival, Greg Norman, was chief executive of LIV Golf until last year.

Court filings show the Australian received $9.4m (£7.2m) in settlement and bonus payments in September 2025.

His successor, O'Neil, received a retention bonus of $6.4m (£4.9m) in June this year.

In September, Norman told The Real Deal with Bob Philion podcast that he was proud of bringing private equity into the sport.

"In a period of basically 2021 to now, close to $8bn (£6.1bn) has been brought into the game of golf," he said.

Responding to those comments, Faldo told BBC Sport: "Eight billion dollars is 8,000 million dollars. If that is a full six years, that is approximately $3.6m (£2.8m) a day.

"Before LIV filed for bankruptcy, seven executives received $15.6m (£11.9m) in retention payments, with further bonuses also paid.

"Now they risk ruining the small businesses that help make their events possible."

BBC Sport has contacted Norman for a response.

'I'm not the one who should feel ashamed'

Companies still owed money include Global Infusion Group, which provided catering at July's LIV Golf UK event and is awaiting £321,671 - which was due on 7 August.

Public records also list more than £3,000 owed to Goodysphere, a family-run Yorkshire firm that provides a sensory bus designed to help autistic children who may find busy events overwhelming.

Just $2m (£1.5m) has been proposed so far by LIV's Saudi owners to pay unsecured creditors, leaving many smaller companies unsure whether they will receive anything at all.

"I've spent months questioning myself, feeling ashamed that our financial difficulties might be perceived as poor management," said Foskett.

"When I look at the billions poured into LIV Golf and the millions reportedly paid to executives, whilst I was personally climbing in and out of skips to meet their zero-waste policy, I've come to realise that I'm not the one who should feel ashamed.

"We didn't invest in LIV Golf. We didn't gamble on its success. We simply went to work.

"Scott O'Neil talks about understanding small businesses. Sir Nick Faldo is standing up for them. Right now, I know whose words mean more to me."

images.caption: Image caption, Sir Nick Faldo's comments follow a BBC Sport investigation
Image caption, Scott O'Neil (right) took over from Greg Norman (left) as LIV chief executive in January 2025

articles.title: Brandel Chamblee Reveals The One Rule Change Needed Before 2028
articles.summary: Brandel Chamblee calls for an end to PGA Tour safety nets, arguing players must prove they belong on the Championship Series. Read his full analysis now.
articles.body:
Brandel Chamblee has issued a sharp call for the PGA Tour to remove the safety nets that allow players to stay on the main tour without proving they can compete. Jimmy Roberts hosted The Big Swing, where the golf analyst discussed 2028 tour structure changes. He argues that the current system lets players rest on past success instead of earning their place through current performance. With former LIV Golf players seeking a return, the tour readies a two-tier split for this debate.

Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm, major champions within the last three years, anchor this conversation. Current plans suggest these men get Championship Series exemptions in 2028 following one-year suspensions. Chamblee rejects this idea entirely and suggests that these players should have to work their way back up from the lower levels of the tour, according to Yahoo Sports . He believes that the sport needs to be more meritocratic and that past glory should not guarantee a future spot.

The Argument Against Lifetime Exemptions

Chamblee's main point is that the PGA Tour has too many protections for players who have lost their edge. Speaking to Jimmy Roberts, he argued for removing safety nets to ensure a fairer environment. The analyst believes that sports must always answer the question of why a specific player is there versus someone else. If greatness five or ten years ago justifies a spot, the system is fundamentally wrong. Golf frequently uses that specific answer to keep players in the lineup, yet it persists.

The current rules allow players with exceptional careers to use one-time exemptions from 2029 onward. This includes players on the top 25 and top 50 of the Career Money List who can elect a one-season exemption if they play enough events. Chamblee sees this as a loophole that undermines the competitive nature of professional sports. He argues that if a player cannot compete, they should be out of the tour. In November 2025, Jordan Spieth and Rickie Fowler faced criticism from fans and fellow players concerning their sponsor exemptions.

The analyst compares the situation to other sports where performance dictates opportunity. Chamblee observes that the performance gap between average and best golfers is far smaller than in baseball. In baseball, the best pitcher can be 20 to 30 percent better than the average player. Scottie Scheffler outperforms the average tour player by merely three and a half percent in golf. Chamblee thinks no golfer deserves a guaranteed spot without current play because margins are so tiny.

Chamblee outlined a harsh reality for stars who left for the breakaway circuit. He stated he would not be surprised if some players must return to the Korn Ferry Tour. They would then have to go to the Challenger Series and work their way into the Championship Series. He emphasized that they should do this because the current system is too easy for them. During his interview, he declared that players must come back and prove themselves. This path would require them to compete against younger players who are fighting for their careers.

This approach contrasts sharply with how the tour has handled players who stayed. Marco Penge almost lost his full PGA Tour card at The RSM Classic, serving as an example. A victory at Sea Island pushed him into the top 100, securing his 2028 Championship Series spot. After winning majors this season, Aaron Rai and Ryan Fox secured exemptions on the Championship Series through the end of 2031. Chamblee highlights that treating those who left differently than those who stayed threatens the game's integrity.

The proposed changes for 2028 include a new two-tier system with promotion and relegation. The top 90 players keep their places, while the top 20 from the Challenger Series get promoted. No alternate list or designated exemptions will exist in the top tier. Chamblee supports this move but wants the rules to be stricter for those returning from LIV. He argues that the tour has a convenient time to do away with these safety nets now that the landscape has changed so much.

Although Chamblee criticizes tour rules, he defended outgoing commissioner Jay Monahan against LIV Golf disruption blame. Brian Rolapp will assume the role on January 1 after Monahan steps down at the end of 2026. Given his nine-year tenure's unique challenges, Chamblee hopes history treats Monahan kindly. He compared the situation to a carmaker giving free vehicles, asking if a rival CEO is bad for losing sales.

Chamblee told The Big Swing that LIV was unique only as a business model ignoring return on investment. He added that no one could have foreseen an irrational actor entering the arena. This perspective suggests that Monahan was reacting to an unprecedented situation rather than making poor decisions on his own. Chamblee believes that Monahan got dealt with the coronavirus pandemic and then LIV back to back.

Despite defending Monahan, Chamblee offered a bleak assessment of sport damage over the past four years. He warned that PGA Tour financial restructuring must not undermine its charitable roots. He thinks people look back and remember this as probably the worst period in golf's history. He is not so sure that this won't echo unfortunately into the future if the philanthropic aspect of the tour is not protected.

Chamblee remains skeptical about the LIV Golf product's long‑term value and its failure to sustain itself. He argues the breakaway circuit failed by trying to manufacture Ryder Cup passion without national pride. LIV golfers played for greed and that was it, Chamblee said. This financial motivation is why the breakaway could not replicate the emotional connection of traditional team events.

The analyst also dismissed the notion that team golf could replicate Ryder Cup emotion globally. He believes that the lack of national pride made it impossible for LIV to build a loyal fan base. The players were not fighting for their countries but for their own financial gain. The tour must ensure that players are there because they are the best, not because they were paid to leave.

Chamblee's comments highlight the deep divide that the LIV saga created within the golf community. Players like Rory McIlroy felt like a sacrificial lamb after leading the charge against LIV. Xander Schauffele also raised doubts about the need for a change in leadership. Tiger Woods stated that what transpired could never happen again. These reactions show the emotional toll the split took on the sport and its players.

The debate over safety nets affects current players who are trying to maintain their status on the tour.

This situation illustrates how the current system allows players to stay on the tour based on past earnings rather than current performance. Jordan Spieth and Justin Thomas, cited by Chamblee as examples of players who are no longer the stars they once were, are highlighted. While he hopes both can regain their peak form, he insists that past success alone should not allow established players to retain their positions. He does not want stars who sort of drop anchor at the top.

Those players dissatisfied with the arrangements must remember they had a chance to profit from the tour's regulations. The door is not open for players who left to just walk back in without proving they still belong.

As the PGA Tour readies for these structural shifts, the 2027 season promises to be very interesting. With the tour scheduled to be divided into two tiers beginning in 2028, attention is already shifting toward the major changes ahead. The narrative surrounding promotion and relegation is intended to become much more prominent. Although players have had many chances to secure a highly advantageous position before 2028, the rules are changing.

Chamblee believes that the time has come for the PGA Tour to get rid of all safety nets that enable players to remain at the highest level long after they have achieved any notable success. He told reporters that eliminating these safety nets is necessary to truly make golf more meritocratic.

A more rigid structure in which performance determines status is likely to be implemented for the tour, and past contributions are less relevant. This shift aims to ensure that the best players are always on the course. Chamblee hopes that the changes will lead to a more competitive and fair environment for all players. Status is dictated by performance under the tour's more rigid structure.
